concepts.title: Optical flow
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow approximates the 2D motion field by measuring displacement of image brightness between two images.
concepts.content: **Optical flow** is an approximation to the 2D motion field computed by measuring displacement of image brightness (@fig-visualization_optical_flow). The ideal optical flow is defined as follows: given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ $\in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3}$, the optical flow $\left[ \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 2}$ indicates the relative position of each pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and the corresponding pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. Note that optical flow will change if we reverse time. This definition assumes that there is a one-to-one mapping between two frames. This will not be true if an object appears in one frame, or when it disappears behind occlusions. The definition also assumes that one motion explains all pixel brightness changes. That assumption can be violated for many reasons, including, for example, if transparent objects move in different directions, or if an illumination source moves.
concepts.motivation_md: Optical flow provides a practical way to estimate apparent motion in image sequences by tracking brightness changes, crucial for motion analysis and scene understanding.
concepts.recap_md:
- Optical flow approximates 2D motion by measuring brightness displacement.
- Defined as pixel correspondences between two images.
- Assumes one-to-one mapping and consistent brightness changes.

concepts.title: When Optical Flow and Motion Flow Are Not the Same
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow may differ from true 3D motion in scenarios like static objects with moving illumination, textureless walls, waves, specular surfaces, and rotating mirrors.
concepts.content:
There are a number of scenarios where motion in the image brightness does not correspond to the motion of the 3D points in the scene. Here there are some examples where it is unclear how motion should be defined:

-   Rotating Lambertian sphere with a static illumination will produce no changes in the image. If the sphere is static, and the light source moves, we will see motion in spite of the sphere being static.

-   Moving in front of a textureless wall produces no change on the image.

-   Waves in water: waves appear to move along the surface but the actual motion of the water is up and down (well, it is even more complicated than that).

-   A rotating mirror will produce the appearance of a faster motion. And this will happen in general with any surface that has some specular component.

-   A camera moving in front of a specular planar surface will not produce a motion field corresponding to a homography.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights situations where optical flow does not reflect true 3D motion, illustrating limitations and ambiguities in motion estimation from image brightness changes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Optical flow may not match 3D motion in complex scenarios.
- Examples include static objects with moving illumination and textureless walls.
- Specular surfaces and rotating mirrors complicate motion interpretation.

concepts.title: The Aperture Problem
concepts.one_liner: The aperture problem occurs when observing motion of a 1D structure larger than the image frame, making it impossible to measure actual motion except orthogonal components.
concepts.content:
One classical example of the limitations of motion estimation from images is the **aperture problem**. The aperture problem happens when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame, as shown in @fig-apperture_problem. If none of the termination points are in view within the observation window (i.e., the aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. Only the component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

(see figure: Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what...)
concepts.motivation_md: The aperture problem illustrates fundamental limits in motion estimation when only partial views of moving structures are available, highlighting ambiguities in perceived motion direction.
concepts.recap_md:
- The aperture problem arises when observing 1D structures larger than the image frame.
- Actual motion cannot be fully measured if termination points are not visible.
- Only motion components orthogonal to the structure can be reliably detected.

concepts.title: smooth prior
concepts.one_liner: Another penalizes variations on the optical flow (smooth prior): $$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}  \right)^2$$
concepts.content:
Another penalizes variations on the optical flow (\textbf{smooth prior}):
$$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = 
\sum_{x,y} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}  \right)^2 +
\left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}  \right)^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: The smooth prior penalizes rapid variations in the optical flow field, encouraging smoother motion estimates that better reflect realistic motion in images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The smooth prior penalizes variations in the optical flow components.
- It is defined as the sum of squared partial derivatives of $u$ and $v$ with respect to $x$ and $y$.
- This regularization encourages smoothness in the estimated motion field.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: If the scene is composed of rigid objects, then we can assume that the motion field within each object will have the form described by equation (@eq-2d_motion_field_from_translation_and_rotation).
concepts.content:
Until now we have not made use of any of the properties of the motion field derived from the 3D projection of the scene. One way of incorporating some of that knowledge is by making some strong assumptions about the moving scene. If the scene is composed of rigid objects, then we can assume that the motion field within each object will have the form described by equation (@eq-2d_motion_field_from_translation_and_rotation).

In this case, instead of a moving camera we have rigid moving objects (which is equivalent). The 2D motion field can then be represented as a collection of superimposed layers, each layer containing one object and occluding the layers below. Each layer will be described by a different set of motion parameters. The parametric motion field can be incorporated into the gradient-based approach described previously. The motion parameters can then be estimated iteratively using an expectation-maximization (EM) style algorithm. At each step we will have to estimate, for each pixel, which layer it is likely to belong to, and then estimate the motion parameters of each layer. The idea of using layers to represent motion was first introduced by Wang and Adelson in 1994 @Wang1994.
concepts.motivation_md: Layer-based motion estimation leverages the assumption that scenes consist of rigid objects, allowing motion to be modeled as layered parametric fields, improving motion estimation accuracy. (book_paraphrased)
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion fields in rigid objects follow a parametric form.
- Motion can be represented as layers, each with distinct motion parameters.
- An EM algorithm estimates pixel-layer assignments and motion parameters iteratively.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Motion estimation is an important task in image processing and computer vision, used in video denoising, compression, and understanding scene dynamics and 3D structure.
concepts.content:
Motion estimation is an important task in image processing and computer vision. It is used in video denoising and compression. In computer vision it is a key attribute to understand scene dynamics and 3D structure. Despite being studied for a long time, accurate optical flow remains challenging, even when using state-of-the-art deep-learning techniques.

The approaches presented here require no training. In the next chapter, we will study several learning-based methods for motion estimation. The approaches presented in this chapter will become useful when exploring unsupervised learning methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding motion is crucial for video processing and scene analysis, but accurate optical flow remains challenging, motivating exploration of learning-based methods. (book_paraphrased)
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion estimation is key for video denoising, compression, and understanding 3D scenes.
- Accurate optical flow remains challenging despite advances.
- Learning-based methods will be explored next.

concepts.title: dense optical flow
concepts.one_liner: We can model motion over time as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ where $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate pixel velocity at $(x,y)$ and time $t$.
concepts.content: We can model motion over time as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$. The quantities $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. The problem with this formulation is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by points in the scene over time. As time $t$ changes, the location $(x,y)$ might correspond to different scene elements.
concepts.motivation_md: Dense optical flow models pixel-wise motion over time, providing a detailed velocity field for each image location, which is crucial for understanding dynamic scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Dense optical flow represents motion as velocity vectors $(u,v)$ at each pixel $(x,y)$ over time $t$.
- It models motion as a sequence of images showing pixel velocities.
- The formulation lacks explicit trajectories for scene points over time.

concepts.title: sparse set of moving points
concepts.one_liner: An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$.
concepts.content: An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$. This has the challenge that we have to establish the correspondence of the same scene point over time (tracking). The appearance of a 3D scene point will change over time due to perspective projection and other variations such as illumination changes over time. It might be difficult to do this on a dense array. Therefore, most representations of motion as sets of moving points use a sparse set of points.
concepts.motivation_md: Sparse sets of moving points simplify motion representation by tracking distinct points over time, avoiding the complexity of dense pixel-wise motion and handling appearance changes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Motion can be represented as a sparse set of moving points (tracks).
- Tracking requires establishing correspondences of scene points over time.
- Appearance changes and perspective effects complicate dense tracking, favoring sparse representations.

concepts.title: brightness constancy assumption
concepts.one_liner: The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time.
concepts.content:
The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time. Mathematically, this assumption translates into the following relationship, given a sequence $\ell(x,y,t)$: 

$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  = \ell(x,y,t)$$

where $u$ and $v$ are the element displacement over one unit of time and are also a function of pixel location, $u(x,y)$ and $v(x,y)$, but we will drop that dependency to simplify the notation. The previous relationship is equivalent to saying that $\ell(x, y, t + 1) = \ell(x-u,y-v,t)$. To make sure that the reader remains onboard without getting confused by the indices and how the translation works, here is a simple toy example of a translation with $(u=1, v=0)$:

(see figure: Translation to the right of a simple $6 \times 6$ size image.)

The constant brightness assumption only approximately holds in reality. For it to be exact, we should have a scene with Lambertian objects illuminated from a light source at infinity, with no occlusions, no shadows, and no interreflections. Few real scenes check any of those boxes. This equation assumes that all the pixels in $\ell(x, y, t)$ are visible in $\ell(x, y, t+1)$, but in reality, some pixels might be occluded in the first frame and new pixels might appear around the image boundaries and behind occlusions.
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption allows relating pixel intensities across frames to estimate motion, simplifying the problem by assuming brightness remains constant despite movement.
concepts.recap_md:
- Brightness constancy assumes pixel brightness does not change as scene elements move.
- Mathematically, $\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1) = \ell(x,y,t)$ relates pixel intensities across frames.
- The assumption is approximate; real scenes have occlusions, shadows, and illumination changes.

concepts.title: Gradient-Based Optical Flow Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Gradient-based optical flow estimation uses a Taylor approximation and the brightness constancy assumption to derive a linear constraint for optical flow at each pixel.
concepts.content:
The most popular version of a gradient-based method for optical flow estimation was introduced by Lucas and Kanade in 1981 @Lucas1981.

Let's start describing the method in words, and we will see next how it translates into math. We will start by approximating the change between two consecutive frames by a linear equation using a Taylor approximation. This linear approximation combined with the constant brightness assumption will result in a linear constraint for the optical flow at each pixel. We will then derive a big system of linear equations for the entire image that, when solved, will result in an estimated optical flow for each image pixel. Let's now see, step by step, how this algorithm works.

If the motion $(u,v)$ is small in comparison to how fast the image $\ell$ changes spatially, we can use a first-order Taylor expansion of the image $\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)$ around $(x,y,t)$:
$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  \simeq \ell(x,y,t) + u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t + \mbox{h. o. t.}$$

Combining equations (@eq-constancy_brightness_assumption) and (@eq-motion_taylor), and ignoring higher order terms, we arrive at the **gradient constraint equation**: $$u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$$

This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ in location $(x,y)$ to be along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell= \left( \ell_x, \ell_y \right)$ at that location. This is the same relationship that we discussed before when describing the aperture problem. This is not enough to estimate motion and we will need to add additional constraints. The second assumption that we will add is that the motion field is constant (or smoothly varying) over an extended image region. By solving for the gradient constraints over an image patch, we hope there will be only a unique velocity that will satisfy all the equations. We can implement this constraint in a different way. One simple way of implementing this constraint is by summing over a neighborhood using a weighting function $g(x,y)$. If $g(x,y)$ is a Gaussian window centered in the origin, the optical flow, $(u,v)$, at the location $(x,y)$ can be estimated by minimizing:
$$\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum_{x',y'} g(x'-x,y'-y) \left| u(x,y) \ell_x (x',y',t) + v(x,y) \ell_y(x',y',t) + \ell_t(x',y',t) \right| ^2$$

The previous equation is a bit cumbersome because we wanted to make explicit the spatial variables, $(x',y')$, over which the sum is being made and the factors that are function of the location $(x,y)$ at which the flow is computed. From now, to simplify the derivation, we will drop all the arguments and write the loss in a single location as:

$$
\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum g \left| u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t \right| ^2
$$
where only $u$ and $v$ are constant.

The solution that minimizes this loss can be obtained by computing where the derivatives of the loss with respect to $u$ and $v$ are equal to zero: 

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(u, v)}{\partial u } =
\sum g \left( u \ell_x ^ 2 + v \ell_x \ell_y + \ell_x \ell_t  \right) = 0 \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(u, v)}{\partial v } = 
\sum g \left( u \ell_x \ell_y + v \ell_y^2 + \ell_y \ell_t  \right) = 0
\end{aligned}$$

We can write the previous two equations in matrix form at each location $(x',y')$ as: 

$$\begin{bmatrix}
\sum g \ell_x ^ 2  & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\
\sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
 u \\
 v
\end{bmatrix}
=
- 
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\
\sum g \ell_y \ell_t
\end{bmatrix}
$$

We will have an equivalent set of equations for each image location. The solution at each location can be computed analytically as $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \textbf{b}$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is the $2 \times 2$ matrix of equation (@eq-lk). The motion at location $x,y$ will only be uniquely defined if we can compute the inverse of $\mathbf{A}$. Note that the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is a function of the image structure around location $(x,y)$. If the rank of the matrix is 1, we can not compute the inverse and the optical flow will be constrained along a 1D line, this is the aperture problem. This will happen if the image structure is 1D inside the region of analysis that will be defined by the size of the Gaussian window $g(x,y)$.

In order to implement this approach we can make use of convolutions in order to compute all the quantities efficiently in a compact algorithm @alg-gradient_algorithm:

concepts.title: Iterative Refinement for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Iterative refinement improves optical flow estimates by minimizing photometric reconstruction error over multiple scales.
concepts.content:
The gradient-based approach is efficient but it only provides an approximation to the motion field because it ignores higher order terms in the Taylor expansion in equation (@eq-motion_taylor). A different approach consists of directly minimizing the photometric reconstruction error:
$$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= 
\sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$

We can now run gradient descent on this loss. Running only one iteration would be similar to the gradient-based optical flow algorithm described in the previous section. However, adding iterations will provide a more accurate estimate of optical flow. At each iteration $n$, the estimated optical flow will be used to compute the warped frame $\ell_1 (x+u_n,y+v_n,t+1)$ and we will compute an update, $\Delta u_n$ and $\Delta v_n$, of the optical flow: $u_{n+1} = u_n+\Delta u_n$ and $v_{n+1}= v_n + \Delta v_n$. To improve the results, the optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid. First, we run a few iterations on the lowest resolution scale of the pyramid (where the motion will be the smallest). The estimated motion is then upsampled and used as initialization at the next level. We iterate this process until arriving at the highest possible resolution. This process is shown in @fig-multiscale_iterative_optical_flow.

@fig-comparison_gradient_vs_iterative compares the optical flow computed using the gradient-based algorithm (i.e., one iteration) and the multiscale iterative refinement approach. Note how the gradient-based approach underestimates the motion of the left car. The displacement between consecutive frames is close to four pixels and that makes the first-order Taylor approximation very poor. The multiscale method is capable of estimating large displacements.

(see figure: Comparison between the optical flow estimated using the gradient-based algorithm and the multiscale iterative refinement approach.)

concepts.title: slow prior
concepts.one_liner: A slow prior penalizes large velocities by regularizing the sum of squared velocity components.
concepts.content:
There are several popular regularization terms. One penalizes large velocities (slow prior): 

$$
R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = 
\sum_{x,y} \left( u(x,y) \right)^2 +
\left( v(x,y)  \right)^2
$$
concepts.motivation_md: The slow prior regularizes optical flow by discouraging large velocity magnitudes, promoting smooth and realistic motion fields.

prereq.rationale: The gradient-based optical flow estimation technique directly uses the brightness constancy assumption to derive the linear constraint for optical flow at each pixel, as described in the passage.
The gradient constraint equation is derived by combining the brightness constancy assumption with the Taylor expansion approximation, directly depending on the definition of brightness constancy.
The gradient constraint equation is a key step in the gradient-based optical flow estimation method, providing the linear constraint used in the system of equations.
Photometric reconstruction error minimization assumes brightness constancy between frames to measure the difference between warped and target images.
The idea that optical flow and motion flow are not always the same depends on understanding the definition of optical flow as an approximation of 2D motion field.
The aperture problem is a limitation in motion estimation from images, which directly relates to the concept of optical flow as an approximation of motion field.

overlay.rationale: The concluding remarks discuss optical flow estimation, which directly relates to the formal definition of optical flow given in an earlier section (48.2). This cross-reference aids understanding of the concept's formal basis.
The iterative refinement method builds upon and improves the gradient-based optical flow estimation by iteratively minimizing photometric error, providing a more accurate estimate.
The slow prior is a regularization term used in optical flow estimation, which complements the brightness constancy assumption by penalizing large velocities.
The smooth prior is another regularization term used in optical flow estimation to penalize variations in flow, complementing the brightness constancy assumption.
Layer-based motion estimation incorporates assumptions about motion fields that can be combined with the brightness constancy assumption in optical flow estimation.
The idea_layer_based_motion_estimation is a narrower restatement or continuation of the same concept as idea_layer_based_motion_estimation__book_c115, sharing the same passage and content.
Dense optical flow is a specific representation of optical flow as a sequence of velocity fields over time, thus a special case of the general optical flow concept.
Sparse set of moving points is an alternative representation of motion compared to optical flow, both modeling motion but with different approaches and challenges.
